verses.text: Now it fell on a day, that Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who bore his armor, “Come, and let us go over to the Philistines’ garrison, that is on the other side.” But he didn’t tell his father.
Saul stayed in the uttermost part of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree which is in Migron: and the people who were with him were about six hundred men;
including Ahijah, the son of Ahitub, Ichabod’s brother, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, the priest of Yahweh in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. The people didn’t know that Jonathan was gone.

Between the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistines’ garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side, and a rocky crag on the other side: and the name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.
The one crag rose up on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man who bore his armor, “Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that Yahweh will work for us; for there is no restraint on Yahweh to save by many or by few.”
His armor bearer said to him, “Do all that is in your heart. Turn and, behold, I am with you according to your heart.”
Then Jonathan said, “Behold, we will pass over to the men, and we will reveal ourselves to them.
If they say thus to us, ‘Wait until we come to you!’ then we will stand still in our place, and will not go up to them.
But if they say this, ‘Come up to us!’ then we will go up; for Yahweh has delivered them into our hand. This shall be the sign to us.”
Both of them revealed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines: and the Philistines said, “Behold, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they had hidden themselves!”

The men of the garrison answered Jonathan and his armor bearer, and said, “Come up to us, and we will show you something!” Jonathan said to his armor bearer, “Come up after me; for Yahweh has delivered them into the hand of Israel.”
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and on his feet, and his armor bearer after him: and they fell before Jonathan; and his armor bearer killed them after him.
That first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armor bearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were half a furrow’s length in an acre of land.
There was a trembling in the camp, in the field, and among all the people; the garrison, and the raiders, also trembled; and the earth quaked, so there was an exceedingly great trembling.
The watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked; and behold, the multitude melted away and scattered.
Then Saul said to the people who were with him, “Count now, and see who is missing from us.” When they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor bearer were not there.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring God’s ark here.” For God’s ark was with the children of Israel at that time.
While Saul talked to the priest, the tumult that was in the camp of the Philistines went on and increased; and Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand!”
Saul and all the people who were with him were gathered together, and came to the battle; and behold, they were all striking each other with their swords in very great confusion.
Now the Hebrews who were with the Philistines before, and who went up with them into the camp, from all around, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
Likewise all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim, when they heard that the Philistines fled, even they also followed hard after them in the battle.
So Yahweh saved Israel that day; and the battle passed over by Beth Aven.

The men of Israel were distressed that day; for Saul had adjured the people, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food until it is evening, and I am avenged of my enemies.” So none of the people tasted food.
All the people came into the forest; and there was honey on the ground.
When the people had come to the forest, behold, honey was dripping, but no one put his hand to his mouth; for the people feared the oath.

But Jonathan didn’t hear when his father commanded the people with the oath. Therefore he put out the end of the rod who was in his hand, and dipped it in the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth; and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the people answered, and said, “Your father directly commanded the people with an oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’” The people were faint.
Then Jonathan said, “My father has troubled the land. Please look how my eyes have brightened, because I tasted a little of this honey.
How much more, if perhaps the people had eaten freely today of the plunder of their enemies which they found? For now has there been no great slaughter among the Philistines.”
They struck the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. The people were very faint;
and the people pounced on the plunder, and took sheep, cattle, and calves, and killed them on the ground; and the people ate them with the blood.
Then they told Saul, saying, “Behold, the people are sinning against Yahweh, in that they eat meat with the blood.” He said, “You have dealt treacherously. Roll a large stone to me today!”

Saul said, “Disperse yourselves among the people, and tell them, ‘Every man bring me here his ox, and every man his sheep, and kill them here, and eat; and don’t sin against Yahweh in eating meat with the blood.’” All the people brought every man his ox with him that night, and killed them there.
Saul built an altar to Yahweh. This was the first altar that he built to Yahweh.

Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night, and take plunder among them until the morning light, and let us not leave a man of them.” They said, “Do whatever seems good to you.” Then the priest said, “Let us draw near here to God.”
Saul asked counsel of God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into the hand of Israel?” But he didn’t answer him that day.
Saul said, “Draw near here, all you chiefs of the people; and know and see in which this sin has been today.
For, as Yahweh lives, who saves Israel, though it is in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.” But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.
Then he said to all Israel, “You be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side.” The people said to Saul, “Do what seems good to you.”
Therefore Saul said to Yahweh, the God of Israel, “Show the right.” Jonathan and Saul were chosen, but the people escaped.
Saul said, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son.” Jonathan was selected.
Then Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done!” Jonathan told him, and said, “I certainly did taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in my hand; and behold, I must die.”
Saul said, “God do so and more also; for you shall surely die, Jonathan.”

The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God today!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
Then Saul went up from following the Philistines; and the Philistines went to their own place.

Now when Saul had taken the kingdom over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, and against the children of Ammon, and against Edom, and against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned himself, he defeated them.
He did valiantly, and struck the Amalekites, and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them.
Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua; and the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal.
The name of Saul’s wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the captain of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul’s uncle.
Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.
There was severe war against the Philistines all the days of Saul; and when Saul saw any mighty man, or any valiant man, he took him into his service.

footnotes.content: Jonathan moves without telling his father—bold, trusting God more than approval. This is how the young sometimes see the Lord most clearly, when they're not waiting for permission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sits under the pomegranate tree in Migron with six hundred men, yet knows nothing of his son's courage. Sometimes the leader is the last to see what God is doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahijah the priest stands ready with the ephod, but the moment belongs to Jonathan. The Lord doesn't always work through the priestly apparatus—He moves through a young man's faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bozez and Seneh—the two rocky crags Jonathan must climb between. Even the landscape tests faith; we remember the names of the places where we risked everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michmash to the north, Geba to the south. The valley between enemy positions is narrow and terrible. But this is where God's work happens—in the tight places where we have nowhere else to look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "There is no restraint on Yahweh to save by many or by few." Jonathan speaks the deepest truth in the book: size doesn't matter to God, only the heart that trusts Him. I wish I'd learned this truth when I was younger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The armor bearer says, "I am with you according to your heart." What a thing to say—to offer not duty but genuine unity. This is how soldiers become brothers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We will reveal ourselves"—no hiding, no scheming. Jonathan and his armor bearer walk into sight of the Philistines. Courage often looks like stepping forward when everything in you wants to shrink back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If they say "Wait," Jonathan will hold his ground and not advance. He's made a covenant with the Lord before the moment arrives. This is how faith works—decide beforehand what you'll trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Come up to us!" becomes the sign. Jonathan is reading the Lord's intention through the enemy's own words. The Lord speaks in many ways if we listen with a quiet heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistines see two men and shout their invitation. They think Jonathan and his companion are refugees crawling out of hiding. The Lord uses even the enemy's contempt to carry out His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh has delivered them into the hand of Israel," Jonathan declares with such certainty that his armor bearer follows him up the cliff. Faith is contagious when it's genuine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Climbing on hands and feet—desperate, real, unarmored and exposed. But the enemies fall before him. Sometimes our weakness is the canvas God paints His strength on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty men in half a furrow's length—a narrow strip of ground, a small number. But enough to change everything. God doesn't measure success the way we do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The trembling spreads—camp, field, garrison, raiders, even the earth itself. One act of faith, one young man trusting God, and the whole system of fear collapses. This is how movements begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul's watchmen see the multitude scatter. While Jonathan acts in faith, his father only watches. Sometimes the one who sees the most is the one who does the least.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul counts the people and finds Jonathan missing. Victory arrives before the king even knows his son's name should be celebrated. This is the shape of tragedy: greatness goes unrecognized by those who should honor it most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul suddenly wants the ark—suddenly remembers God. But he reaches for the apparatus of faith only after the work is done. We do this too: pray after we should have trusted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tumult grows while Saul consults the priest. The Lord is already moving; consulting takes time we don't have. Sometimes faithfulness means letting go of needing to be in control.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistines strike each other in great confusion—the Lord's work of deliverance. Enemies destroy themselves when panic takes hold. This is how battles are sometimes won before the Lord's people even arrive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebrews who had defected to the Philistines now turn to fight for Israel. One act of faith awakens loyalty in the hearts of the wavering. Courage is catching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men hiding in the hill country emerge to join the battle. They had retreated in fear; now they follow hard. The Lord stirs courage in hidden places when He sees one person stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh saved Israel that day"—the turning point. God's salvation doesn't wait for perfect preparation or full armies. It comes when there's a heart ready to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul binds the people with an oath: no food until evening. Victory is already won, but Saul is still commanding, still controlling. Some leaders can't stop leading even when God has taken over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Honey on the ground—plenty, natural provision, a gift. The land offers its sweetness to the weary soldiers. But Saul's oath blocks them from receiving it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people see the honey dripping but touch nothing. Their fear of the oath is stronger than their hunger. This is how legalism works: obedience becomes joyless, and provision becomes forbidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan alone tasts the honey because he didn't hear his father's command. His eyes brighten—literally, life returns. The man who trusts God finds freedom where others find only rules.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Someone tells Jonathan of Saul's oath. The soldier who should celebrate becomes weak. Guilt is a terrible teacher when the law is the master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan speaks plainly: "My father has troubled the land." The son sees what the father cannot—that his order was wrong. Sometimes the young have clearer sight than those in power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "How much more if the people had eaten freely?" Jonathan's logic is sound: rest feeds strength. The refusal of provision limits victory. Some of us learn this too late in life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michmash to Aijalon—the whole region turned back against the Philistines. The battle spreads as hunger spreads weariness through the people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people pounce on the plunder and eat meat with blood—hunger wins, the law breaks. Extremity teaches us what we really believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sees the violation and acts swiftly, but the correction comes too late. The people had to break the law to restore themselves. Legalism creates the very disorder it fears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Saul orders the proper way: bring the animals, kill them here, eat without blood. Authority can correct its own rules, but it often waits until harm is done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "This was the first altar that Saul built." A king finally remembers to honor the Lord—but only after Jonathan has already won the battle. The best deeds sometimes go unmarked by those in power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul wants to pursue all night, but the priest says "Let us draw near here to God." Leadership that forgets to consult the Lord will eventually stumble. The priest's restraint is wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul asks God directly, but receives no answer. The Lord's silence speaks volumes. When we've built a pattern of not listening, God sometimes lets the silence teach us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul gathers everyone to find who sinned. His suspicion turns the army into investigators. Authority driven by fear always becomes suspicious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Though it is in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die."—readers today hear an echo in the way we sometimes declare judgment too quickly on the faithful. Looking back, I see now how often the faithful are condemned by those who command, not by those who truly know the Lord's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul divides the people to find the guilty one by casting lots. A system of ritual replaces the conscience. This is how just men become unjust—through procedure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Show the right." The lots choose Jonathan. The apparatus of divination works—and condemns the righteous. Sometimes the tools themselves are neutral; it is the hand wielding them that is guilty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan is selected by lot. Fate falls on the faithful one. The irony is cold: the son who saved Israel is now marked for death by the father's own decree.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan confesses simply: "I tasted a little honey. Behold, I must die." No defense, no excuse. The righteous often face judgment with more grace than their judges wield it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You shall surely die." Saul pronounces the death sentence on his own son without hesitation. This is how kingdoms rot from within—when the leader loves order more than family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people rise up: "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation?" They see what Saul cannot: value is not measured by obedience to an oath, but by faithfulness to God's work. The people rescue their hero.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul stops pursuing the Philistines. The moment of prayer and judgment has ended. Jonathan lives, but his father's heart has shown its true face. Some wounds don't heal between fathers and sons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul fights all his enemies on every side and defeats them. The external victories continue, yet the internal corruption spreads. A kingdom can win battles while losing its soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did valiantly—delivered Israel from plunderers. Saul's valor is real, his victories authentic. But valor without wisdom is a slow catastrophe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan, Ishvi, Malchishua; Merab and Michal. The names mark a family, a lineage. Yet Jonathan's shadow falls longer than the others—he is the one history remembers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahinoam, the wife; Abner, the commander. Saul's household is complete, his authority established. But the best of what he has—his son Jonathan—remains estranged.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The genealogy shows Abner is Saul's cousin. Blood ties bind the court, yet cannot heal its wounds. Family connection alone is not enough when the heart is bent toward jealousy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Severe war against the Philistines all the days of Saul." The conflict never ends because Saul is always fighting—enemies without and, increasingly, the truth within. The restless warrior never finds peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
